activities.anchor: a worker needing six weeks off after surgery may be FMLA-eligible
activities.caption: three requests, three statutes
activities.name: hrLeaveBranch

config.root: Three requests land on your desk the same morning. Which law answers each?

start.text: The HR arithmetic is genuinely case-by-case.

choices.label: Six weeks off after surgery
choices.feedback: Leave-law territory: 12 weeks of job-protected unpaid leave — for covered employers, with a year of service and 1,250 hours worked.

choices.label: A permanently modified schedule
choices.feedback: An accommodation case: the ADA's open-ended duty to adjust the job, schedule or equipment, absent undue hardship.

choices.label: Indefinite leave
choices.feedback: Where both statutes famously run out — the interactive process, documented meeting by meeting, is what the law actually examines.

fmla.text: 12 weeks, job-protected, unpaid — then the conversation changes.

ada.text: Reasonable accommodation has no fixed end date — the duty runs as long as the person is qualified and the hardship is not undue.

indef.text: No statute answers 'how long is forever?' — this is where process is protection, in writing.

config.why: Leave law works in weeks; the accommodation duty works open-ended — and the case law lives in the space between them.

activities.anchor: that employment law only bans deliberate prejudice
activities.caption: drag the divider — practice, then measurement
activities.name: hrStructuralCompare

config.prompt: What the practice looks like, and what the law measures — drag the divider:

before.label: The neutral-looking rule
before.text: Diploma filters, tenure-based pay, blanket criminal-record exclusions, a model trained on biased history.

after.label: What creates the liability
after.text: Measured impact falling on protected groups without job justification — disparate impact is arithmetic, and the burden shifts to the employer.

config.why: Compliance is a statistics-and-validation discipline, not a purity-of-heart exercise — which is exactly why HR exists as a profession rather than a policy memo.

activities.anchor: HR's central tension is built into the job description
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the dual loyalty
activities.name: hrLoyaltySpot

config.prompt: One line of this trust summary is wrong — click it:
lines: Employees must believe HR will handle a harassment complaint lawfully and confidentially.
Leadership must believe HR will keep confidences and enforce standards even when the subject is a star performer.
What HR owes a whistleblower versus the employer is a recurring dilemma.
When a credible safety threat emerges, confidentiality outranks the duty to act.
The law sets the floor, the code sets the professional standard, and process is protection for everyone.
config.correction: Confidentiality must yield to a duty to act — credible safety threats and harassment the organisation is legally required to address.
config.why: HR is paid by the employer while safeguarding employees' rights — the profession's central tension, resolved by ethics codes and, ultimately, the law.

activities.anchor: HR is the employee's confidential advocate
activities.caption: true or false — what HR owes you
activities.name: hrAdvocateJudge

statements.s: What you tell HR stays between you and HR, like a doctor or a lawyer
statements.why: The function's loyalty is dual by design: it is paid by the employer, and a credible complaint creates a legal duty to investigate and act that no confidentiality promise can suspend.

statements.s: HR can be fair, professional and genuinely protective of your rights
statements.why: That is the accurate model — a professional inside the organisation, not your private counsel.

statements.s: HR exists to protect the employer from employees, full stop
statements.why: HR serves the employer while safeguarding employees' rights — both sides at once, or neither works.

statements.s: Professional codes exist because the function's value depends on trust on both sides
statements.why: SHRM's code — professional responsibility, fairness and justice, conflicts of interest — is the standard above the legal floor.
